result:
**The proposed answer of 98 is wrong.** The argument for it does not match the actual condition for Ana to win, and a counting bound rules out 98.

**Reformulating the condition.** Let X be Ana's set of integers. Banana's observation is a vector v = (f(x_i)). A vector v is consistent with prime p exactly when x_i ≡ x_j (mod p) forces v_i = v_j, and f is nonconstant. For a pair of distinct primes p, q, Ana wins only if no vector is consistent with both.

- **Connectivity.** If the join of the partitions "mod p" and "mod q" on X has at least two classes, Banana takes v nonconstant on X, constant on join classes. This v is realised by a nonconstant period-p function and by a nonconstant period-q function, so Ana fails. Hence the join must be a single class.
- **Coverage.** If the join is a single class, v must be constant on X. Banana then needs a residue mod p missed by X (and likewise mod q) to make f nonconstant. So for every pair, at least one of p, q must have all its residues covered by X.

**Counting bound.** Consider the bipartite graph whose vertices are the residue classes mod p and mod q that X meets, with one edge per x_i joining its two classes. Connectivity forces at least (number of vertices − 1) edges. If both p and q are fully covered, this gives n ≥ p + q − 1.

At most one prime below 100 can be uncovered, so there are two cases:
- If 97 is the uncovered prime, the pair (89, 83) gives n ≥ 89 + 83 − 1 = 171.
- If 89 is the uncovered prime, the pair (97, 83) gives n ≥ 179.
- If any smaller prime is uncovered, the pair (97, 89) gives n ≥ 185.

So n ≥ 171 in every case. Since 98 < 171, the value 98 cannot be the minimum.

The proposed reasoning also has a gap: it never justifies why n = 98 would suffice, and it does not address the pairwise connectivity requirement at all. The claimed "interval of 98 consecutive integers" fails, since it cannot give the required connectivity for the large prime pairs.

I did not determine the exact minimum here. The bound above shows only that it is at least 171.

VERDICT: REJECT
